segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Once he was praying in a certain place, and when he had finished, one of his disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “When you pray, say: ‘Father, may your name be held holy. May your kingdom come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Give us each day our daily bread.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And do not bring us into testing.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Suppose one of you has a friend and goes to him at midnight and says to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for a friend of mine has arrived at my house from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And suppose he answers from inside, ‘Do not bother me. The door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will get up and give him as much as he needs.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And I tell you: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which of you fathers, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead of a fish?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If you then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now he was driving out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the man who had been mute spoke, and the crowds were amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons, that he drives out the demons.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Others, testing him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I drive out the demons by Beelzebul.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if I drive out the demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if it is by the finger of God that I drive out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the strong man, fully armed, guards his own estate, his possessions are left in peace.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when someone stronger than he comes against him and overpowers him, he takes away the full armor on which he had relied and distributes his spoils.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none, it says, ‘I will return to my house that I came out of.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then it goes and brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they go in and settle there. And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Blessed is the womb that carried you, and the breasts that nursed you!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the crowds were growing larger, he began to say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For just as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The queen of the South will be raised at the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and look—something greater than Solomon is here.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they turned back at the proclamation of Jonah, and look—something greater than Jonah is here.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on the lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Your eye is the lamp of the body. When your eye is generous, your whole body is full of light; but when it is evil, your body is full of darkness.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: See to it, then, that the light in you is not darkness.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If then your whole body is full of light, with no part of it dark, it will be full of light all over, as when the lamp shines on you with its brightness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had finished speaking, a Pharisee asked him to have a meal with him, so he went in and reclined at the table.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisee was amazed when he saw that he did not first wash before the meal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Lord said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Fools! Did not the one who made the outside make the inside as well?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But give what is inside as charity, and look—everything is clean for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every garden herb, yet you pass over justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the seat of honor in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked tombs, and the people who walk over them do not know it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the experts in the law answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us too.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woe to you experts in the law as well! For you load people with burdens hard to carry, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets, and it was your ancestors who killed them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you are witnesses and approve of the deeds of your ancestors: they killed them, and you do the building.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason the Wisdom of God also said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute,’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that this generation may be called to account for the blood of all the prophets poured out since the foundation of the world,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, this generation will be called to account for it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not go in yourselves, and you hindered those who were going in.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he went out from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to oppose him fiercely and to question him closely about many things,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: lying in wait to catch him in something he said.

notes.phrase: may your name be held holy
notes.note: Traditionally “hallowed be your name,” using an English verb now rarely met elsewhere. The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy” and, with God’s name as its object, means to treat or acknowledge as holy. The meaning is not in dispute; the choice of English is one of clarity.

notes.traditional: Our Father which art in heaven
notes.note: Luke’s form of the prayer is shorter than Matthew’s. Many later manuscripts expand it to match Matthew, reading “Our Father in the heavens” and adding “may your will be done” and “rescue us from the evil one.” The earliest witnesses have the short form translated here, and most scholars regard the longer readings as harmonizations.

The Greek adjective is almost unknown outside the Lord’s Prayer, and its meaning is genuinely uncertain. The main proposals are “for the coming day,” “necessary for existence,” and “for today.” The traditional “daily” is kept because no alternative is secure; most translations do the same and give the other options in a footnote.

Traditionally “temptation.” In the usage of the period, including the Greek Old Testament, the word mainly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful; modern “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin and can suggest that God lures people into wrongdoing. Lexicons recognize both senses and scholars disagree about which is in view here, so this is an editorial choice. Most versions keep “temptation,” and some have “time of trial.”

Traditionally “importunity” or “persistence.” In the usage of the period the word means lack of shame, brazenness, and there is little evidence that it meant persistence as such; the petitioner is shameless in knocking at midnight. Some scholars instead refer “his” to the man in bed, who acts to avoid being shamed, but most take it of the one asking.

notes.traditional: a house divided against a house falleth
notes.note: The Greek is terse and can be read two ways: houses collapsing onto one another, as a picture of a kingdom laid waste, or “a house divided against a house falls,” matching the parallel sayings in Matthew and Mark. The translation takes the first, which follows the Greek wording more simply; a number of versions take the second.

Traditionally “repented.” “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek verb in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct—which is what the people of Nineveh do in the book of Jonah. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

Traditionally “single” or, in modern versions, “healthy.” The Greek word means single or sound, but its opposite in this saying, an “evil” eye, was a known Jewish idiom for stinginess, so the good eye is taken here as a generous one. Most translations keep the physical image with “healthy” and mention generosity in a footnote, and in Luke’s setting, where the subject is how people respond to Jesus, many interpreters think soundness or sincerity is the main point.

The Greek verb is the one usually rendered “baptize”; here it has its ordinary sense of immersing or washing. The issue is not hygiene but the ritual washing before meals that Pharisees observed as part of their purity tradition.

notes.phrase: give what is inside as charity
notes.traditional: give alms of such things as ye have
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and its sense is disputed. It may mean giving the contents of cup and dish to the poor, or giving from what is within oneself, that is, from the heart; some take it as “give what you have.” The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

Under the Law, contact with a grave made a person ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), so burial places were marked to warn passersby. The charge is that the Pharisees, who prized purity, spread defilement to people who never notice it.

Traditionally “lawyers.” The word names specialists in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with the scribes; “lawyer” now suggests an attorney representing clients in court. Several modern versions use “expert in the law” or something close to it, while others keep “lawyer.”

No such saying is found in the Jewish Scriptures or in any other surviving text. It may come from a lost writing, or “the Wisdom of God” may be a way of speaking of God’s purpose or of Jesus himself; in Matthew’s parallel Jesus speaks the words in his own person. It is also uncertain where the quotation ends; the translation closes it at the end of this verse.

notes.phrase: from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah
notes.note: Abel is the first person murdered in Scripture (Genesis 4). Zechariah is usually identified with the priest stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22. In the traditional Hebrew ordering of the books Chronicles stands last, so the two names would span the whole of Scripture, though that ordering cannot be proved for the first century.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels and Revelation, and translators split between the archaic “woe to you” and paraphrases such as “how terrible for you,” so one decision is needed.
Recurs in Matthew, Luke and Acts, and versions vary between “alms,” “charity,” and “giving to the poor”; “alms” is archaic and readers would be confused by variation.
The standard exorcism verb throughout the Gospels and Acts, rendered variously “cast out,” “drive out,” and “expel”; it should be uniform.
Very frequent, and translators alternate between “evil,” “wicked,” and “bad,” which also affects the “evil eye” idiom and “the evil one.”
Frequent in the Gospels, and versions divide between “scribes” and “teachers of the law,” which overlaps with the register’s “expert in the law” for νομικός.
